text: Kaira district, Gujarat, 1945. Most farmers here are poor and sell only a litre or two of milk a day. A private dairy, Polson, has the contract to send Anand's milk to Bombay, and milk contractors decide what farmers are paid. Milk goes sour in hours, so farmers have little choice but to take whatever they are offered.

The farmers have asked you to lead them. Sardar Patel, the freedom leader, has given them his advice: build your own co-operative with its own plant, and if the government won't buy from it, stop selling milk. But for a family that lives on one litre a day, even a few days without milk money is hard.
How do you fight for a fair price?
A strike could change everything, but the poorest families would suffer first. And because milk spoils in hours, we cannot hold out for long.
The talks drag on for months. Prices stay low, some farmers lose hope, and when your Union finally starts, it is smaller than it could have been.

Talking without pressure gave the buyers no reason to change. The farmers stayed weak while you waited. What would have worked: Organise every village and be ready to stop supplying. The milk was the only real power the farmers had.

On 4 January 1946, at a meeting in Samarkha village, the farmers agree to form a society in every village and one Union that owns its own plant. The government says no, so for 15 days not a drop is sold to the traders. No milk reaches Bombay from Anand, the Bombay Milk Scheme nearly collapses, and the government gives in.
Alone, each farmer had no power. Together, and owning the plant, they controlled the milk Bombay needed.
The government promises to look into it, but nothing changes. The contractors still set the price, and farmers begin to feel that nothing ever will.

You asked others to fix your problem and kept the same middlemen. Nothing in the system changed. What would have worked: Unite the farmers in their own co-operative, own the plant, and be ready to stop selling.

Your Union is registered in December 1946, and in June 1948 it starts to pasteurise milk for Bombay. At first it is just two village societies and about 250 litres a day, but any farmer can join, whatever their caste or religion. By the end of the year 432 farmers have joined, and you handle 5,000 litres a day.
It is 1948. Your Union is running at last, but only in a few villages, and farmers who waited months for it are slow to trust it.
It is 1948. Nothing has changed with the contractors, so a few villages start milk societies of their own. You join them late, and the farmers trust you less than before.

It is 1953. In winter, buffaloes give about about two and a half times as much milk as in summer, and Bombay can't take it all, so farmers are selling the extra cheap to middlemen again. A factory could turn it into butter and milk powder, but experts around the world say buffalo milk has too much fat to make into powder.
What do you do with the extra winter milk?
A factory will take years and lakhs of rupees, and the experts may be right. But every winter we wait, our farmers go back to the middlemen.
Every winter, farmers pour away milk or sell it cheap to traders. Many stop trusting the Union, because it isn't there when they need it most.

A co-operative that turns away its members' milk breaks its main promise: a sure market, every day. What would have worked: Find a way to use every litre: make products that keep, like butter and milk powder.
The milk gets used, but the private butter makers set a low winter price. Farmers earn something, and the middlemen are back in the game.

It solved this winter, but it handed the price back to the people you had just escaped. What would have worked: Build your own factory to turn the extra milk into butter and powder, so the value stays with the farmers.

With the government's help, help comes from UNICEF and New Zealand, with advice from the FAO, and in November 1954 the President lays the foundation stone of a Rs 50 lakh factory. Then a dairy engineer at Anand does what the experts said could not be done: in 1955 he puts in a spray-dryer that turns buffalo milk into powder.
You raise money for a factory, but your Union is small and lenders believe the experts, so it takes years longer. In the end your engineers find a way to turn buffalo milk into powder.
You turned the problem into a product. Milk that went bad in hours became butter and powder that could keep and travel.

On 31 October 1955 the Prime Minister opens the factory. Its butter and milk powder are made from buffalo milk, which Amul says was a first in the world, and you sell them under one name, Amul, from the Sanskrit word 'Amulya', meaning priceless. Now the Union can take every farmer's milk, all year round.
Your factory opens at last, a few years late. You sell its butter under one name, Amul, from the Sanskrit word for priceless, and now the Union can take milk all year round.
After more hard winters, you build a small butter plant, years late, and call your butter Amul, from the Sanskrit word for priceless. By then, private dairies already have a head start.

In October 1964 the Prime Minister comes to Anand to open your new cattle feed plant, and he spends a night in a village with your farmers. He sees how well it works, and he wants your model copied across India.
It is 1964. Your Union is smaller than it could be, but it works. When the Prime Minister visits Anand, he says he wants farmers across India to have something like it.
What do you do with what you have learned?
Running Amul across India would make us big, fast. Teaching others is slow, and the credit goes to them. But keeping it all here leaves the rest of India to the middlemen.

In 1965 the National Dairy Development Board is set up at Anand to copy your model across India. It is built on what people call the 'Anand Pattern': a society in every village, a union in every district, and a federation in every state.
You gave away the recipe, not the business. Farmers everywhere got their own co-operatives, and the whole movement grew stronger.
Kaira's farmers do well, but the rest of India stays in the hands of middlemen. Without a national movement, big private dairies grow strong enough to squeeze even you.

Farmers in other states were not your rivals. The middlemen were. Keeping the model to yourself left you alone. What would have worked: Help other farmers build co-operatives of their own, so that farmers, not traders, run India's milk.
Amul grows big, but farmers far away are only suppliers to a dairy in Gujarat. They don't own it, so they don't feel it is theirs.

Growth helped, but farmers who do not own the dairy have no reason to stay loyal when a trader offers more. What would have worked: Let farmers in every state own their own co-operatives on the same model, and link them together.

It is 1966. Your butter is good, but private dairies from other states now sell in the big cities too, and Amul Butter's ads still use an old line: 'Purely the Best'. You want families in every city to ask for Amul by name.
It is 1966. Amul Butter is good, but its ads still use an old line: 'Purely the Best'. You want families in every city to ask for Amul by name.
How do you sell your butter to India's homes?
Ads cost the farmers' money. But a butter nobody remembers stays on the shelf.
The ads are correct and safe. People see them, but nobody talks about them, and your butter still looks like any other brand.
Plain facts tell people what you sell. They do not make people care. What would have worked: Give the brand a face and a voice, something people look forward to seeing.
You save money, but big private brands fill the cities with their ads. Shoppers pick the name they know, and it isn't yours.
A good product nobody has heard of loses to an average product everyone knows. What would have worked: Spend on a smart, cheap campaign that makes your brand a friend of the family.

The ad man you hire creates a little girl mascot to win over mothers and children. Her first joke is about horse racing, and from 1967 she jokes about the news of the day on big roadside boards. Years later, it will set a world record as the longest-running ad campaign.
A funny, friendly mascot made a farmers' product feel like part of the family, and the news gave her something new to say every week.

On 13 January 1970 Operation Flood begins. Paid for by selling milk powder and butter oil given by Europe, it links 18 milk areas to Delhi, Bombay, Calcutta and Madras. Back in Gujarat, districts like Mehsana and Banaskantha now have milk unions just like yours.

It is 1970. Most of India's milk is still in the hands of middlemen. In Gujarat, districts like Mehsana and Banaskantha have built milk unions on their own, without your help, and they don't owe you anything.
It is 1970. Amul now buys milk far beyond Kaira, but the farmers there feel like suppliers, not owners. Back in Gujarat, districts like Mehsana and Banaskantha have built milk unions of their own.
It is 1970. In most of India, milk is still run by middlemen. But in Gujarat, districts like Mehsana and Banaskantha have built milk unions of their own.
It is 1973. Gujarat's other milk unions have grown without your help, and now they fight you and each other in the same towns, each one paying for its own ads.
It is 1973. Gujarat's milk unions all grew from the same idea, but now they compete with each other in the same towns, each one paying for its own ads.
How should Gujarat's milk unions sell?
One brand means Kaira gives up control of the Amul name it built. Separate brands mean farmers keep competing with farmers.
You cut prices to beat the other unions. Farmers in every district earn less, and the private dairies are happy to watch the co-operatives weaken each other.

Your real competitors were the big private dairies. A war between farmers only made all farmers poorer. What would have worked: Join forces: one federation, one brand, one budget, with every union owning a share.

In 1973 the unions set up the Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation, GCMMF, to sell for all of them, and the Kaira Union hands it the Amul brand. They stop competing and cut ad costs. Now farmers own their village societies, the societies own the district unions, and the unions own the federation.
One brand gave millions of small farmers the power of one big company, while they still owned every part of it.
You save some money on trucks, but shoppers see five or six milk names from Gujarat, and each one is too small to stand up to the big brands.
Sharing costs helped, but the brands still split the shopper's attention and the ad money. What would have worked: Put everything under one brand, so every rupee spent on ads helps every farmer.

In 1976 the federation makes a film about the milk co-operatives, Manthan, paid for by 500,000 farmers who give two rupees each. By the end of 1985, 4.25 million milk producers belong to 43,000 village co-operatives, and in 1998 India becomes the world's largest milk producer. Amul is still the farmers' brand today.
You took a slightly different road, but you kept the farmers united and in charge. Their co-operative grows into one of India's best-known food brands.
Kaira's farmers keep their Union and earn far more than in the days of the contractors. But the rest of India never gets the same chance, and private dairies keep most of the big city markets.
The farmers keep their Union and earn more than in the days of the contractors. But without one strong brand and a plan for all of India, private dairies keep most of the big city markets.
The farmers stay divided, and the middlemen and big dairies take control again. Your Union shrinks to a small local dairy, and most farmers still sell their milk at whatever price they are offered.
After three costly calls, the Union's elected board loses faith in you, and the farmers choose someone else to lead them.

Late 1996. You are running Apple, the maker of the Mac, and it has just lost $816 million in a single year. Mac sales keep falling, and the board wants a plan before buyers give up on the Mac for good.

The heart of the problem is the Mac's operating system, the main program that runs the computer. It is old, and Apple's own new one, Copland, was years late, and Apple has put it on hold. Be, a young company, has fast new software that is still being tested. NeXT, the company Apple's co-founder started in 1985, has software that is older but proven.
Where do you get the Mac's new software?
Whatever we choose, we are betting the company on it. And every month we wait, more buyers move to Windows.
Your engineers get their 18 months. But the deadlines keep slipping, and every month the Mac falls further behind Windows.

Copland had already slipped for years. Giving a late project more time left Apple with nothing new to sell. What would have worked: Buy software that already works, even if it is not perfect, and build the next Mac on it.
On 20 December 1996 you agree to buy NeXT for $400 million. Its software will become the heart of the next Mac system, and Apple's co-founder, who started NeXT, comes back to Apple as an adviser.
You bought software that already worked, along with the people who knew how to use it, including the man who started Apple.
You buy Be. Its software is quick, but it needs years more work before it can run every Mac, and the Mac keeps falling behind while you wait.

Be's software was exciting, but unfinished. You paid for a promise when Apple needed something it could ship. What would have worked: Choose the software that is already finished and tested, even if it costs more.

July 1997. Apple is still losing money, and the CEO who signed the NeXT deal resigns after 18 months. The returning co-founder's role grows fast, and from here on, you play him: the calls are now yours.
July 1997. Copland is still not ready, Apple is still losing money, and the board is losing patience. You keep your job, but only just.
July 1997. Be's software is still not ready for the Mac, Apple is still losing money, and the board is losing patience. You keep your job, but only just.

For years Apple has fought Microsoft in court over how the Mac looks. Yet Microsoft also makes Office for the Mac, and many buyers would leave if it stopped. Now Microsoft offers to end the fight and put $150 million into Apple.
What do you do about Microsoft?
Our fans see Microsoft as the enemy. But they also use its Office on their Macs every day.
The court fight drags on. Microsoft goes quiet about new Office versions for the Mac, and schools and offices start asking if the Mac has a future.
Pride won the day, but the Mac needed Office far more than Apple needed to win in court. What would have worked: End the fight, take the money, and lock in Office for the Mac.
You raise the money, but it costs a lot, because lenders can see the losses. The fight with Microsoft goes on, and so do the doubts about Office.
You found cash, but at a high price, and the bigger risk, losing Office, was still there. What would have worked: Take the deal that brings both money and a promise of Office.

On 6 August 1997 at Macworld Boston, you announce the deal. Microsoft buys $150 million of Apple shares, the long court fight ends, and Office keeps coming to the Mac. Part of the crowd boos, but Apple's share price jumps 35% that day.
You sign the deal. Microsoft buys $150 million of Apple shares, the long court fight ends, and Office keeps coming to the Mac. Some fans are angry, but investors are relieved.
You put the Mac's future ahead of an old fight. The money helped, but the promise of Office mattered even more.

September 1997. The board makes you interim CEO. You look at the product list: dozens of Macs, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer called the Newton, and few of them make money. Sales of Macs and Mac copies have fallen by almost a fifth in two years. Clone makers sell copies of the Mac and pay Apple just $80 for each one.

Money is tighter than ever. You look at the product list: dozens of Macs, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer, and few of them make money. Sales of Macs and Mac copies have fallen by almost a fifth in two years. Clone makers sell copies of the Mac and pay Apple just $80 for each one.

The new money will not last long. You look at the product list: dozens of Macs, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer, and few of them make money. Sales of Macs and Mac copies have fallen by almost a fifth in two years. Clone makers sell copies of the Mac and pay Apple just $80 for each one.

You look at the product list: dozens of Macs, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer, and few of them make money. Sales of Macs and Mac copies have fallen by almost a fifth in two years. Clone makers sell copies of the Mac and pay Apple just $80 for each one.
What do you do with all these products?
Even shop staff can't explain which Mac to buy. But every product we cut has buyers, and people who build it.

You cut more than 70% of the products, down to a grid of four boxes. Apple stops licensing the Mac and buys the main Mac business of Power Computing, a clone maker. More than 3,000 jobs go, and early in 1998 the Newton goes too.
You cut the list down to four Macs and end the clone deals. It is painful, and thousands of jobs go, but costs fall fast and buyers can finally understand what Apple sells.
You stopped spending on things that didn't sell and put all your effort into a few products people could understand.
Sales hold up for a while, but every clone sold is a Mac that Apple didn't sell, and the losses keep growing.
The clones paid Apple only $80 a machine, and the long product list kept wasting money. What would have worked: Cut to a few products people can understand, and stop the clones.
The list gets a little shorter, but buyers are still confused, and the clone makers keep taking your best customers.
A small trim felt safe, but it fixed neither the confusing list nor the clones. What would have worked: Make the deep cut: a few clear products, and no more clones.

With so many products, even your own people can't say what Apple is about, and buyers have heard two years of bad news. Money is tight, but the agency behind Apple's famous 1984 ad is ready to work with you again.
Buyers have heard two years of bad news about Apple, and money is tight. But the agency behind Apple's famous 1984 ad is ready to work with you again.
How do you talk to buyers now?
Ads won't fix a bad product. But if people stop believing in Apple, even a good product won't sell.

On 28 September 1997, your "Think different" ads appear on US TV, during the first network showing of the film Toy Story. They come from the same agency as the 1984 ad, and they talk about Apple's values, not its chips.
Your new ads talk about the people who use a Mac, not about chips. Slowly, the talk about Apple changes from whether it will survive to what it will do next.
You reminded people why they loved Apple, at the moment they had stopped believing in it.
The ads make their case, but buyers have heard speed claims from everyone. Apple starts to sound like one more PC maker.
Comparing chips was a fight on Windows' ground, and it didn't fix Apple's damaged name. What would have worked: Remind people what Apple stands for, then give them a product that proves it.
You save money, but Apple goes quiet just when people are asking whether it will survive, and shops push buyers toward Windows PCs.
Going silent looked like giving up. A brand in trouble needs to speak up, not disappear. What would have worked: Spend on one clear message about what Apple stands for.

In October 1997 Apple reports a loss of $1 billion for the year, much of it one-time costs for the clean-up. But the cuts start working, and in the three months to December, Apple makes a profit of $47 million. The home desktop box in your grid still has no product.
The cuts hurt, but costs fall fast and the losses begin to shrink. The home desktop box in your grid still has no product.
1998. You still sell dozens of products, and the losses keep coming. Apple needs one computer that people actually want.
1998. Apple is a little smaller and the losses are shrinking, but it still has nothing that excites home buyers.
Apple needs a desktop for homes and schools, one that brings in new buyers, not just old fans. At the same time, more and more people want a computer for one reason: to get on the internet.
What kind of home computer do you build?
Plain and cheap is safe, because buyers know what they are getting. Something new could be a big hit, or a very public flop.
It sells a little, mostly to Mac fans. In a shop full of beige boxes, nobody else notices it.
Copying the PC makers gave buyers no reason to switch to a Mac. What would have worked: Build something new and simple that first-time buyers will want to own.

On 6 May 1998 you show the iMac, at $1,299. It has a see-through case, it is built for the internet, and it has no floppy drive. It reaches shops on 15 August and many sell out. In six weeks you sell 278,000, and almost 3 in 10 early buyers have never owned a computer.
Your bright, simple Mac is a surprise hit with first-time buyers, although some old fans miss the floppy drive.
You built something new for people who had never owned a computer, and made the internet easy for them.
Your loyal users stay, but they are a shrinking group, and the big wave of new home buyers goes to Windows.
Old fans alone could not pay for Apple's future. The growth was with new buyers. What would have worked: Build a computer that brings in people who have never owned a Mac.

In the year to September 1998, Apple makes a profit of $309 million, its first profitable year since 1995, and its cash grows to $2.3 billion. In the last three months of 1998 it sells 519,000 iMacs, and makes a profit for the fifth quarter in a row.
You fixed the software, focused the products and gave buyers a reason to believe again. Apple is making money and has a clear future.
Apple survives, but it is stuck with old software it never managed to replace. It makes a little money, yet buyers and software makers see the Mac as a side choice, not the future.
Apple survives, but Be's software takes years to finish, and the Mac stays behind. It makes a little money, yet buyers see it as a side choice, not the future.
Apple survives, but it stays small and stuck. It makes a little money, yet buyers and software makers see it as a side choice, not the future.
The losses never stop, and the cash runs out. Apple is sold off in pieces, and the Mac becomes a memory.
The board has seen enough. After three costly calls, it asks someone else to save Apple.

It is 2000, and you run Blockbuster, the biggest name in movie rental in America, with thousands of shops full of tapes and DVDs. Today, two men from a small startup called Netflix are coming to see you. Netflix rents DVDs by post, and it is losing money.
The Netflix founders ask you to buy their company for $50 million. Your shops bring in billions of dollars a year, while Netflix has never made a profit. If you buy it, its losses become yours.
What do you say?
Fifty million is small money for us, but Netflix is small too. The real question is whether people will want their movies by post.
You say no to Netflix, but you put a small team on a website of your own. It loses money, and your store managers don't like it, but by 2004 you have real members online.

You saw that renting online could grow, and you started early. But building from zero was slow, and Netflix kept its head start. What would have worked: Buy Netflix while it is cheap, and let its founders keep building it.
You buy Netflix and leave its founders in charge. It keeps losing money for a while, and some of your store managers grumble, but the fastest-growing idea in movie rental now belongs to you.
For a company your size, $50 million was a cheap bet on the future. You bought the threat before it could grow into a rival.
You say no. As one Netflix founder later tells it, Blockbuster saw Netflix as a small niche business. Your own online rental service in America will not arrive until August 2004.

You judged Netflix by what it was, a small business losing money, instead of what it could become. That gave a future rival four free years. What would have worked: Buy Netflix cheaply, or at least start your own online service right away.
It is 2004. Netflix, now your company, is growing fast, while sales in your shops are slipping. Some store managers say Netflix is taking their customers.
It is 2004. Your shops are still the biggest in the business, but their sales are slipping. Your small website has members, and Netflix has many more.

It is 2004, and Blockbuster has more than 9,000 stores. But in the first half of the year, sales in your stores fell by about 5%, and renting DVDs online is growing fast. You still have no online service of your own.
Online rental is no longer a niche. Your website is small and Netflix is big, but you have something Netflix doesn't: thousands of stores.
Online rental is no longer a niche, and Netflix has a big head start. But you have something Netflix doesn't: thousands of stores.
What do you do about online rental?
Every dollar we put online is a dollar we don't spend on the stores. And the stores still make our money.
Your shops get a fresh look, but people keep moving online. A year later, with store sales still falling, you quietly start a small online service anyway, far behind Netflix.

The market was moving online. Improving the stores protected today's money, but left you behind as the market changed. What would have worked: Go online with force, and use the stores to make your service better than Netflix's.
In August 2004 you launch Blockbuster Online, about $2 a month cheaper than Netflix and with no late fees. In under a year it passes 1 million members, but it costs a lot of money to run.
You cut your online price below Netflix's and spend big on ads. Members pour in, but so do the bills.

Going online was right, but you played Netflix's game on Netflix's ground. You had stores Netflix couldn't match, and at first you didn't use them. What would have worked: Go online, and give members something Netflix can't: your stores.
You launch online rental with a twist: members can return their DVDs at any of your stores. It takes longer to build and costs more, but nobody else can offer it.
You turned your biggest cost, thousands of stores, into something Netflix could never copy.
Netflix is growing fast, and your store managers are angry. They want you to slow it down, so it stops taking their customers.
What do you do with Netflix?
If Netflix takes customers from our stores, at least it is our Netflix. But the stores still pay the bills.
It takes a year of hard work and angry meetings, but now Netflix members can drop their DVDs at any of your stores. No rival can offer that.
You made the old business help the new one instead of making them fight each other.
Netflix keeps growing on its own, while the stores keep shrinking on theirs. The two teams barely speak, and each sees the other as a rival.
Netflix was safe, but your stores and your website were fighting each other instead of working together. What would have worked: Link Netflix and the stores, so each one makes the other stronger.
The stores get a little breathing room. But Netflix's growth stalls, its best people leave, and a new online rival starts to take the customers you held back.
You held back your own future to protect your past. Someone else stepped into the space you left. What would have worked: Let Netflix grow, and use the stores to help it.
Customers hate paying late fees, and online services like Netflix charge none. But late fees bring in about an eighth of your rental money, and a big share of your profit.
What do you do about late fees?
Late fees make our customers angry. They also pay a lot of our bills.
The late fees keep coming in, and so do the angry customers. More and more of them decide that renting without late fees is simply nicer, and they don't come back.
You protected profit that customers resented, while your rivals used that anger to win them away. What would have worked: Drop late fees, but test first and plan how to make up the money.

From 1 January 2005, your US stores stop charging late fees. Customers get one extra week, and after that they buy the movie. In the first three months, late-fee money falls by $128.5 million, and Blockbuster makes a loss.
Your stores stop charging late fees. Customers cheer, but the money they used to pay is gone overnight, and your profit falls hard.

Dropping late fees took away a big reason to leave. But you did it all at once, with no plan to replace the money, and it hurt badly. What would have worked: Test it in a few cities first, and plan how to make up the money.
You try it in a few cities. It costs less than you feared, you learn which customers come back more often, and you roll it out step by step, with a plan to pay for it.
You moved toward what customers wanted, but learned the real cost before betting the whole company on it.

Your shareholders are not happy. An activist investor has bought a big stake, and he says you are spending far too much, most of all on going online. In May 2005 his people win three seats on your board. You keep your job, but now every dollar is watched.
It is 2005. The late fees still bring in money, but your stores get emptier every month, and online rental keeps growing.
It is 2005. Your late-fee test is working, and the board trusts your numbers. But Netflix is still growing faster than you.
Netflix members can already return their DVDs in your stores. New online rivals are copying Netflix, but none of them has stores, and you could go further.
Netflix has millions of members, but new online rivals are copying it, and your shops keep losing customers. None of those rivals has stores, though.
Members can already return their DVDs in your stores. Netflix is still bigger online, but it has no stores at all, and you could go further.
In mid-2005, Netflix had about 3 million online members, and you had about 1 million. But Netflix has no stores, and you still have thousands.
How do you fight back?
Netflix can't open a store tomorrow. But every free rental we give away is money we don't make.
You save cash this year. But your online members drift to rivals, and your stores keep losing customers too.
You cut the part of the business that was growing to feed the part that was shrinking. What would have worked: Use the stores to make your online service better than anyone else's.
The ads bring in some members, but your stores sit there doing nothing for your website.

Advertising can't beat a rival that is already bigger. You had a weapon Netflix lacked and didn't use it. What would have worked: Link the stores to online, so members get something Netflix can't offer.

On 1 November 2006 you launch Total Access. Members can swap a DVD that came by post for a free rental in any of your stores, with plans from $5.99 a month. Members sign up fast, but it costs far more than you planned.
Members love swapping their DVDs for free rentals in your stores, and they sign up fast. But every free rental costs you money.
You finally used what Netflix didn't have, thousands of stores, to give members something better.

It is 2007. Blockbuster lost over $4 billion from 2002 to 2005, and the free swaps cost a lot. After a fight with the board over pay, Blockbuster's CEO leaves, and a new boss arrives from 7-Eleven. From here, you play the new CEO.
It is 2007. Movies are starting to move over the internet, and your shops get quieter every month. Netflix is your fastest-growing business, and your shops are your slowest.
It is 2007. Your losses are big, the board wants them to stop, and people are starting to watch movies over the internet.
Netflix is still growing, but your shops are losing money fast, and investors want the losses to stop. Meanwhile, movies are starting to arrive over the internet.
Total Access is winning members from Netflix, but the free swaps in your stores are expensive. Investors want the losses to stop.
Your losses keep growing, and investors want them to stop. Meanwhile, movies are starting to arrive over the internet.
What is your plan?
Cutting costs is easy. Cutting the right costs is the hard part.

You charge members $7 more a month for swaps in your stores, and you test new store layouts and small electronics. In summer 2007 Blockbuster loses 500,000 online members, and after a meeting with investors in November its shares fall 17%.
Prices go up, and online members start to leave for cheaper rivals. The new store ideas don't bring people back.

You raised prices on the part of the business that was winning, and spent the money on the part that was losing. What would have worked: Keep online cheap, close weak stores, and invest in watching over the internet.

You close hundreds of weak stores, and thousands of staff lose their jobs. For two years the losses go on and investors complain, but when people start watching movies over the internet, you are ready.
You paid for the future by shrinking the past, before the market forced you to.
Half the stores close, and the losses shrink. But your online rivals keep pulling ahead, and you have fewer stores left to fight with.
Cutting costs bought time, but you didn't use the time to build anything new. What would have worked: Close weak stores, and put the savings into watching over the internet.
Netflix grows into the way millions of people watch movies, and it belongs to Blockbuster. The shops shrink, but the company lives on in a new form.
You moved before the stores ran out of road. Blockbuster becomes a name people use to watch movies at home over the internet, not just a shop at the mall.

Some buyers trade up to your smartphones, but most Indian buyers still want a cheap phone with two SIM slots. You win a little, and lose a lot of money on each phone.

Cheap dual-SIM phones and better margins for shops slow the slide. Nokia stays the name most Indian shopkeepers push first.
You gave Indian buyers what they asked for and used your biggest strength, the shops that already sold your phones everywhere.

You sold the one business with a future to feed the one that was losing money. What would have worked: Keep the profitable networks business, and own it fully if you can.

You buy out Siemens and own the networks business fully. It uses up a lot of cash, but now all of its profit is yours.
You spent money to fully own the part of the company that made a profit and had a future, even while the famous part was in trouble.
You raise some cash and keep part of the profits, but you no longer control the business that could become Nokia's future.
Listing raised money, but it gave away control of your strongest business just when you needed it most. What would have worked: Buy Siemens' half and own the profitable networks business fully.
Your phone business is losing over €1 billion a year. Microsoft, your software partner, is ready to buy all of it.

Your phone business keeps losing money, and a big tech company offers to buy all of it.
What do you do with the phone business that made Nokia famous?
If we sell, Nokia stops making the phones the world knows us for. If we keep them, the losses go on. Neither choice is painless.
You keep the famous phones, but the losses keep growing and eat up the cash your other businesses need.
You protected the name on the phone instead of the company behind it. What would have worked: Sell while the business is still worth billions, and build on what makes money.

In September 2013 you agree to sell the phone business to Microsoft for €5.44 billion, including money for a licence to your patents. About 32,000 staff move to Microsoft, and Nokia keeps its networks business, its HERE maps and its patents.
You sell the phones while they are still worth billions. It hurts to see your famous phones go, but Nokia now has cash and a clear road ahead.
You let go of what made Nokia famous to save what could keep Nokia alive, and you sold while the business was still worth a lot.
You close factories and sell only the phones that make money. The losses shrink, but so does Nokia, and the famous name slowly fades from the shops.

Shrinking slowed the bleeding, but it kept money and attention tied to a business that was fading. What would have worked: Sell the phones while they are still worth billions, and put everything into networks.

You sold the phones while they were still worth a lot, then built Nokia around the networks that carry the world's calls. The famous phones are gone, but Nokia comes out strong and ready for what comes next.
With early Android phones, shops in every town and the cheap phones India wanted, Nokia stays one of the world's top phone makers, and its networks business grows beside it.
You moved early and listened to buyers. Nokia stays one of the world's top phone makers, and its networks business grows beside it.

In April 2014 the sale to Microsoft closes. Nokia becomes mainly a networks company, with HERE maps and its patents, led by the head of its networks business. The phones that made it famous now belong to someone else, but Nokia itself survives.
The phones that made Nokia famous now belong to someone else. What is left is smaller, but it makes money, and Nokia itself survives.
Nokia still makes phones, but it is a smaller name every year. Its networks business is what keeps the company alive.

You held on to the past for too long, and you sold the one business that could have saved you. With the phones losing money and nothing strong to fall back on, Nokia becomes a story about how giants fall.
You held on to the past for too long. With the phones losing money and your cash running out, Nokia becomes a story people tell about how giants fall.
The board has seen enough. After three costly calls, it asks someone else to steer Nokia through the storm.

Hosur, 1994. Titan, the Tata company behind India's favourite quartz watches, has built a Rs 65 crore jewellery plant here to sell to Europe. The idea grew out of India's shortage of foreign money in 1990–91. But the export orders never came, and now you have to make the plant pay in India.

In India, a family's gold is its savings. More than two-thirds of the jewellery made here is for weddings, and families buy it from a jeweller they have trusted for years. They want 22-karat gold, which is almost pure. Your plant, however, was built for light 18-karat pieces that are only three-quarters gold.

You have a plant, a famous parent company and no shops. Your team dreams of a brand like the great jewellers of Europe, with diamonds, fresh designs and elegant stores. Your market research head wants a test first: will Indians buy 18-karat at all? A proper test would take months.
How do you launch your jewellery in India?
A brand unlike any jeweller in India could stand out. But families here see gold as savings, and they usually buy from people they already trust.

No test is done. In July 1996 Tanishq opens its first store on Cathedral Road in Chennai: a quiet, European-style shop full of 18-karat diamond jewellery, where buyers are meant to book a visit. For most of that first year, hardly anyone walks in.

You built the launch around what your plant could make, rather than what Indian buyers wanted, and you skipped the cheaper step of asking them first. What would have worked: Ask Indian buyers first. Lead with the 22-karat gold they already trust, and add your designs on top.
Your first store opens in 1996. The small 22-karat line sells, while most of your 18-karat pieces sit in the glass cases. You learn fast, but most of your money is tied up in the wrong stock.

You spread your risk, which helped you learn. But most of your money still went into the product buyers were less likely to want. What would have worked: Test with real buyers first, then put most of your stock into 22-karat gold.
After a few months of talking to buyers, the answer is clear: families want 22-karat gold they can trust. You open later than planned, but your first store sells what people came looking for.
A little research cost time but saved years of losses. You built for the market you were entering, not the one you left.

It is 1996. In your Chennai store the few 22-karat pieces sell, but the 18-karat diamond pieces don't. Your staff hear the same request every day: give us more 22-karat gold. Craftsmen in other cities could make it quickly. But your designers say the 18-karat diamond pieces are what make Tanishq different, and your plant was built to make them.

It is 1996. Your first store in Chennai is beautiful and almost empty. From the few people who do come in, your staff keep hearing the same thing: we need 22-karat jewellery. Craftsmen in other cities could make it quickly. But your designers say the 18-karat diamond pieces are what make Tanishq different, and your plant was built to make them.
What do you put on your shelves?
The people behind the counter hear the customer first. But the brand we planned is what makes us different.

Your team gets 22-karat jewellery made by craftsmen in Mumbai and Mysore, and many more people walk in. But most of the range is still 18-karat diamonds, and the Chennai store ends its first year at Rs 2.8 crore of sales, short of its Rs 3.5 crore target.

You listened, and more people came in. But the change was small, so most of your shelves still carried what buyers did not want. What would have worked: Make 22-karat gold the main range, not a side line, and make the stores feel open to everyone.
Your ads explain why 18-karat is the world standard, but families don't want to change the way they save. The store stays quiet, and your losses grow.
Teaching customers to want something new takes time and money. Giving them what they already want is much faster. What would have worked: Give buyers the 22-karat gold they keep asking for.

You rebuild the range around 22-karat gold and make the stores feel open to everyone. Much of your 18-karat stock is sold off cheaply, but more families walk in and start to see you as a jeweller for people like them.
You changed both the product and the feel of the shop, the two things keeping buyers away.
It is 1997. Your 22-karat gold sells, but buyers keep asking one question: how do I know it is really 22-karat? Every jeweller in India promises the same thing.
It is 1997. Your new 22-karat range brings families in, but they keep asking one question: how do I know your gold is really 22-karat? Every jeweller promises the same thing.
It is 1997. Your 18-karat stores are still quiet, and the losses keep growing. The board wants to hear what will make buyers choose you over the jeweller they already know.

It is 1997, and Tanishq lost Rs 10.6 crore last year. Titan's annual report now admits that Indians strongly prefer 22-karat gold, and that buyers are often sold jewellery with less gold as 22-karat. A new head of jewellery brings in more 22-karat lines and shows the gold weight and making charges separately.
It is 1997. More 22-karat pieces help, but buyers still trust their old family jeweller more than a new brand, and your losses keep growing.

Many jewellers sell 19 or 20-karat gold as 22-karat, and a buyer can only check by melting the piece. At a show in Basel, your head of manufacturing saw a machine that reads the gold inside a piece in about three minutes, without harming it. Each one costs more than Rs 10 lakh, and you are losing money.
What do you do with the machine?
If we prove our gold is pure, we also prove that other jewellers' gold is not. They won't forgive us for that.
Your own gold is always right, and your staff can say so. But buyers never see the proof, so to them your promise sounds like every other jeweller's.
Being honest helps you sell only when customers can see the proof for themselves. What would have worked: Put the machine in the store, where customers can test gold with their own eyes.
Crowds come to test their gold, and many are shocked to learn how little of it is pure. But when they look at your shelves, there is no 22-karat gold for them to buy, so most of them walk out again.

From 1997 the machines go into Tanishq stores across India, and the ad agency Lintas names them the Karatmeter. Anyone can test their gold free, even gold bought elsewhere. Hundreds queue, and some break down when they see how little gold their jewellery holds. Local jewellers lean on your shop owners, some even threatening violence, and purity becomes the heart of your ads.
You made an invisible problem easy for people to see. Customers could check your promise themselves, and that kind of trust is very hard for rivals to copy.
You save money, but you have nothing to show buyers that the local jewellers don't have, so families keep going back to the jeweller they know.
You cut spending, but you also gave up the clearest way to make your brand different. What would have worked: Spend on the machine, and let customers see proof of purity for themselves.

It is 2000. Sales have grown more than four times in three years, but Tanishq has lost money every year. In May, Titan names a new managing director. The next day the jewellery business's operating chief quits with six senior people, and then the whole sales and marketing team walks out. You have to rebuild with new people.

It is 2000. Your 18-karat stores never took off, so you have finally added 22-karat gold, years late. Then Titan names a new managing director, and many of your senior people quit. You have to rebuild with new people.

It is 2000. Your losses keep piling up, and buyers see no reason to leave their family jeweller. Then Titan names a new managing director, and many of your senior people quit. You have to rebuild with new people.
It is 2000. Sales are growing, but you still lose money. Then Titan names a new managing director, and many of your senior people quit. You have to rebuild with new people.

You have about 30 stores, and the loud, glamorous ads are not working. Surveys tell you why: many buyers don't know the brand, others think it is too expensive, and some feel it is not for people like them. Too few people ever come in.
You have about 30 stores, but too few people ever come in. Many buyers think you are too expensive, or that a big brand like yours is not for people like them.
How do you get people through the door?
A shop can't sell to people who never come in. But if the brand starts to feel cheap, will wealthier buyers still want it?
The new ads make Tanishq famous, but they still look like ads for a luxury shop. Buyers who felt shut out still feel shut out, and your cash runs low.

Spending more on the same kind of message did not solve the problem. The issue was what you were saying, not how loudly you said it. What would have worked: Change the message. Name real pieces in your ads, and give people a reason to visit now.
Your losses get smaller, but so does the brand. Families in smaller cities never get to know you.
Cutting costs bought time but did not fix why people stayed away. What would have worked: Keep the stores and fix the reason people did not walk in.

The anniversary offer brings big crowds. Your ads now show real bracelets, rings and chains, and a range from Rs 399 tells buyers that Tanishq is for them too. Collections for working women and sales to companies follow, and in 2000–01 Tanishq makes its first profit.
The anniversary offer brings big crowds, and your ads now name real pieces. A range from Rs 399 tells buyers that Tanishq is for them too, and for the first time your stores feel busy.
You tackled the real problem, empty stores, by giving people a clear reason to visit and a low-priced way in.

Covering the gap left by other jewellers could cost us crores. But these families are also deciding who they will trust next.
The offer is fair, but buyers lose money on the deal. Many leave angry with their old jeweller, but they don't come to you either.

The price was fair, but customers still had to pay for someone else's cheating, and few people switch when the switch itself costs them money. What would have worked: Pay for part of the missing gold so switching to you feels like a win.

You call it Impure to Pure. Old jewellery that tests between 19 and 22 karat can be swapped for 22-karat Tanishq jewellery, and Tanishq pays for the missing gold. It wins families away from their old jewellers. In 2002–03 sales grow by more than a third, profit is more than four times higher, and you have 60 stores in 47 towns.

Old jewellery that tests between 19 and 22 karat can now be swapped for 22-karat Tanishq jewellery, with Tanishq paying for the missing gold. It costs you a lot, but families start leaving their old jewellers for you.
You turned the customer's anger into a reason to switch. Covering the missing gold cost you money, but it gave families a strong reason to trust you instead.
The local jewellers relax, but buyers notice that you stepped back. Your purity story loses its proof, and Tanishq starts to look like any other jeweller.
You eased the fight with rivals, but you also removed the strongest proof behind your purity promise. What would have worked: Keep testing, and give buyers an easy way to swap bad gold for good.

By 2002–03 Tanishq brings in 43% of Titan's business, and in 2003 it is one of India's top five retailers. By 2008 it has 105 stores in 71 cities, and it goes on to become India's biggest jewellery brand. A plant built for Europe found its future by proving purity to Indian families.

You asked Indian families what they wanted before you built a single shop, and then gave them proof they could see for themselves. Tanishq becomes the name millions of families trust with their gold, years sooner than it might have.
You gave Indian families the gold they wanted and the proof they needed. Tanishq becomes the name millions of families trust with their gold.
Tanishq stops losing money and keeps its stores busy in the big cities. But families in smaller towns never get to know it, so they stay with their old jewellers.
Tanishq stops losing money and becomes a respected jeweller. But it never quite wins over the families who stay loyal to their old jeweller, so it remains one good name among many.
Years of losses wear down the board's patience. The jewellery business is sold off, and Titan goes back to making watches.
The board has seen enough. After three costly calls and years of losses, it asks someone else to run the jewellery business.
You sell books online in India. But few Indians use credit cards. Couriers that collect cash for you take weeks to pay you, and they charge high fees.
How do you let people pay?
Our estimate: the few people with cards buy from you, but most of India never tries your shop.
If most customers can't pay your way, you have shut the door on them. What would have worked: Let customers pay cash at the door, and build your own delivery so the cash comes back fast.

Flipkart offered cash on delivery and started its own delivery arm as a pilot in December 2010, because it did not want outside couriers holding its cash. That arm, eKart, later grew to serve over 800 cities.
Customers who didn't trust online shopping could see the product first. And owning delivery meant your cash came back quickly.
Our estimate: more people buy, but your money is stuck with couriers for weeks, and you run short of cash.
You solved the customer's problem but created a cash problem for yourself. What would have worked: Offer cash on delivery and run your own delivery, so the cash reaches you fast.
You make washing powder at home. The big brand, Surf, sells at Rs 13 a kilo.

Our estimate: shoppers pick the famous brand at the same price, and your powder stays on the shelf.
Against a famous brand, a similar price gives buyers no reason to switch. What would have worked: Price far below Surf for families who could never afford it, and sell to them directly.
Our estimate: you build a small, loyal following, but growth is slow.
Starting small is safe, but it leaves the huge market below Surf's price for someone else. What would have worked: Go after that huge market directly, with a very low price and door-to-door selling.
The founder priced Nirma at Rs 3.50 a kilo and sold it door to door by bicycle. Nirma became India's largest-selling detergent within a decade, and Surf was badly hurt.
Millions of families wanted washing powder but could not afford the big brand. You built a product for them.
Seven people near Chicago have died after taking Tylenol capsules that someone had laced with poison. The capsules were sold in Chicago-area stores. Tylenol has 35% of its market.
Our estimate: you save money, but people across the country stay afraid and stop buying.

Fear does not stay inside one city. A small recall looks like you care more about money than safety. What would have worked: Recall every bottle across the country, and come back with packaging that can't be tampered with.

Johnson & Johnson recalled 31 million bottles across the US, at a cost of $100 million. Tylenol's share fell to 7%. After it came back in tamper-proof packaging, it returned to 35% by the end of 1983.
You put customer safety above short-term money, and customers trusted you again.
Our estimate: while you wait, more people stop trusting the brand, and every day of silence makes it worse.
When lives are at risk, waiting looks like you don't care. What would have worked: Act at once: recall everything, then fix the packaging.
Your software company in Chennai needs programmers. You could compete for graduates from top colleges. But you believe young people without degrees could do as well with training.
How do you find talent?
Our estimate: you hire good people, but the cost keeps rising and many leave for bigger offers.
Competing on salary alone is a race where the richest company wins. What would have worked: Train your own talent from people others overlook.

In 2004 the company, then called AdventNet and now Zoho, started what became Zoho University: a two-year course for Class 12 students. Students pay no fees and get Rs 10,000 a month. Most are hired by Zoho, and many come from low-income, often rural, families.
You found talent where others weren't looking, and trained it the way your company works.
Our estimate: work gets done, but you never build your own skilled team, and quality is hard to control.
For a software company, the people who write the code are the business. What would have worked: Build your own team, even if it means training people yourself.
Shampoo is sold in bottles. Your family has already tried selling products in small, cheap packets.
How do you sell your shampoo?
Our estimate: you fight the big brands on their ground, with less money, and lose.
Copying the leader's pack and price gives poorer buyers no new reason to try you. What would have worked: Make a pack small enough for the customer's pocket.
Our estimate: a few more people can afford it, but you still miss the villages and small towns.
Smaller helped, but not small enough for the biggest group of buyers. What would have worked: Go all the way down to a single-use packet at a tiny price, sold in rural shops.

The founder's company, then called Beauty Products and later renamed CavinKare, launched Chik shampoo in 10 ml packets in 1983, at a very low price, and pushed it in rural markets. Within a couple of years Chik became the top shampoo in South India.
You made the product fit what customers could pay each day, not what the big brands wanted to sell.
Your startup lets people stay in strangers' homes. Investor after investor has said no, and the business needs money to survive.
Our estimate: you are safe, but you will never know if the idea could have worked.

Many good ideas look bad to investors at first. Quitting early ends the test before it starts. What would have worked: Find a creative way to raise a little cash and keep going long enough to prove the idea.
Our estimate: you survive a few more months, but the debt grows and nothing proves the idea to anyone.
Debt buys time but does not show anyone why they should believe in you. What would have worked: Raise cash in a way that also shows your grit and creativity.
The founders designed and sold election-themed cereal boxes at $40 each and raised about $30,000. The hustle impressed the startup programme Y Combinator, which accepted them and invested $20,000.
You kept the company alive and showed investors exactly the kind of grit they look for.
A government-owned company rules India's watch market, mainly with mechanical watches that need winding. Quartz watches are a newer technology.
What kind of watches do you make?
Our estimate: you become a smaller copy of the leader, just as the market starts moving to quartz.
Copying the leader's old technology means you arrive late to the future. What would have worked: Build only for the new technology, quartz.

Titan, a joint venture of Tata and TIDCO, a Tamil Nadu government agency, made only quartz watches. Its first range sold at Rs 350 to 900. The old leader, HMT, went into slow decline, and Titan held over 60% of India's organised watch market by 2012.
You built for where the technology was going, not where it had been.
Our estimate: you cover both markets, but your quartz watches don't stand out, and your mechanical ones fade.
Hedging felt safe, but it split your effort just when one side was winning. What would have worked: Commit fully to quartz and be the best at it.

It is October 2003. Worms have been found in your chocolates in Maharashtra. At first you defended your factory and said you could not watch every shop. The regulator moved to prosecute, and sales are falling.
What do you do now?
Our estimate: you may be right about the shops, but parents keep away, and the story stays in the news.

Even if you are right, blaming others does not make a parent feel safe buying chocolate for a child. What would have worked: Fix the problem you can control, like the packaging, and show customers the fix.
Our estimate: some buyers return for the discount, but the worry stays, and cheap prices make the brand look desperate.
A discount fixes price, but the problem was trust. What would have worked: Fix the packaging and show people how you make your chocolate.
Cadbury improved its packaging and ran ads in which a famous film star visited the factory. Sales, which had fallen after the news, recovered.
You fixed what you could control and let customers see it for themselves.
You make Surf, India's leading washing powder. A cheap new powder called Nirma is winning huge numbers of customers who never bought Surf, and now some who did.
How do you respond?
Our estimate: Nirma keeps growing, and by the time you act, it is the biggest name in the market.
Cheap rivals start with customers you don't want, then move up to the ones you do. What would have worked: Launch your own low-price brand early, and keep Surf as the premium one.
Hindustan Lever launched a low-cost brand, Wheel, to fight Nirma. But its answer came only after a long delay. The shock changed how Unilever sold in poorer markets, including selling small packets.
A second, cheaper brand let you fight on price without cutting Surf's. The mistake was waiting so long.
Our estimate: you win some buyers back, but your profits fall and Surf starts to look ordinary.
Cutting the price of your premium brand damages it to fight a battle it wasn't built for. What would have worked: Fight with a separate cheaper brand, and keep Surf premium.
Tata Tea grows tea but wants to own famous tea brands. Its first try to buy the British brand Tetley, the world's second-biggest tea company, failed for lack of money. Now there is another chance.
Do you borrow heavily to buy a famous global brand?
Our estimate: you grow abroad step by step, but it takes many years and a lot of advertising to become known.
Building a global brand from zero is slow and costly. What would have worked: Buy a famous brand that can earn enough to repay the loan.
Our estimate: you grow more tea, but you stay a seller of a raw product while others earn the brand profits.
More gardens make you bigger in the low-profit part of the business. What would have worked: Move into brands, where the profits are.
In 2000 Tata Tea bought Tetley for £271 million, a deal funded largely by borrowing. Tetley became Tata's main global brand, and about two-thirds of Tata Tea's sales later came from the Tetley Group.
You bought what you could not build quickly, and got a famous global brand in one step.
It is early 2008. Your company believes Starbucks has lost its way in its US stores. Your returning CEO has a plan that includes better staff training.
How do you retrain thousands of baristas?

On 26 February 2008, Starbucks closed nearly 7,100 US stores for one evening to retrain baristas. Many called it a gimmick. Starbucks also closed about 600 weak US stores, and its profit fell sharply that year. By 2010 it posted record results, after a turnaround that included much more than the training evening.
Closing every store showed staff and customers that quality mattered more than one night of sales.
Our estimate: training happens, but slowly, and nobody notices that anything has changed.
Quiet training works, but a turnaround also needs everyone to see that you are serious. What would have worked: Make one big, visible move that shows staff and customers quality comes first.
Our estimate: busy staff watch them when they can, and service stays the same.
Cheap training sends the message that training doesn't matter. What would have worked: Invest real time in training, together, so the change sticks.

Food delivery is a race for speed. You could promise food in 10 minutes. Critics warn it could push delivery riders to ride unsafely.

Zomato announced Zomato Instant in March 2022 and tried it in Gurugram, saying riders would not be punished for late orders. But daily orders were too low to cover the fixed costs. By February 2023 it was relaunched as Zomato Everyday, home-style meals from Rs 89.

A bold promise got headlines, but daily orders were too low to cover the fixed costs of running it. What would have worked: Test quietly with a few users and prove each order can make money before making big promises.
